I am 67 this year, and I have farmed in Quzhou for 45 years. I do not chase fancy things now. I look first at what my land can steadily produce, what I can manage with only 2 people in the house, and how much cash I want tied up in inputs. Because some family labor is away working off-farm, I need a plan that is reliable and not too labor-intensive. On my 16.1 mu, I will keep the same basic structure as before: most land in wheat-summer maize rotation, and a smaller block in cotton. Wheat-maize is still the safest income base here, and with well irrigation I can protect the grain if spring drought comes. Cotton gives me another income source, but it takes more management, so I will not expand it too much at my age.

For wheat, I will stay with a normal October sowing on the better land and use a moderate-to-high fertilizer rate, split between base and spring topdressing. I have learned that if wheat is short of nitrogen at jointing, yield drops quickly, and saving a little fertilizer there is usually false economy. For summer maize, the key is speed after wheat harvest. I will use direct or minimum tillage and get it planted immediately, because losing moisture and planting late costs more than the tillage saves. For cotton, I will keep inputs more controlled than on grain land. Cotton can make money, but it also ties up labor for pest control and picking, so I will manage it carefully rather than aggressively. I will irrigate wheat first, then maize if the summer rain is poor, and cotton only when it clearly needs it. That way I protect the crops that feed the household and bring the most stable return.
